Proficiency in the Term 1 listening/turn-taking conventions plausibly supports success in the broader Term 4 conversational engagement, so buildsTowards first_to_second. judgment.rationale: Both Skills sit in Grade 1 (coordinate rank 1, resolved), Term 1, Skill Area WRITING, and are printed in the same table row (row=3, window 16, page 63) under two distinct sub-strands: 'Handwriting' (f505b10f...) for the first and 'Shared, Group and Independent Writing' (dc5d3c66...) for the second, per the singleton merge reasons which explicitly treat them as separate co-listed sub-strand headings. The first requires tracing over, copying and writing one's own name from a template with starting point and direction indicated (LCs: tracing, copying, writing own name from template; tags handwriting, letter formation, template). The second requires writing words using letter sounds learnt (LC 'Writes words using sounds learnt'; tags phonics, letter sounds, words, writing). These are substantively coherent complementary components of early written production in the same term - legible letter formation alongside encoding words from taught sounds - so this is meaningful instructional coherence rather than generic repetition or mere shared wording. However, buildsTowards is not supported: the endpoints share the same grade rank and the same term, so a developmental claim needs substantive pair-specific evidence of extension, and none is present. The target's defining demand is grapheme-phoneme encoding knowledge that the source does not develop, while the source's defining demand is directional letter formation of one template-scaffolded word (the learner's own name); neither is a scaled version of the other along a shared dimension, and CAPS presents them as concurrent Term 1 requirements rather than a sequence. Accordingly the symmetric relatesTo with null direction is recorded, preserving canonical endpoint order. Limitations: both endpoints have truncated source evidence (24 omitted items each) and all endpoint and ancestor nodes carry upstream audit/merge context (including the merged Grade 1 and Term 1 banner nodes), so the judgment rests only on the bounded statement text, Learning Components and supplied hierarchy; these warnings are retained and not resolved here.

Shared LC tags 'phonics' and 'word recognition' corroborate the same decoding strand, so Grade 2 proficiency in the split digraph plausibly supports success with the wider Grade 3 silent-letter set. They share substantive conceptual coherence around early print awareness - that written marks/letters stand for language (one from the production side, one from the print-concept/reading side, LC tags 'emergent writing/copying/letters/own name' vs 'emergent reading/print awareness/spoken words/written words'). The evidence does not, however, show that copying one's own name is a capability whose proficiency materially supports understanding speech-to-print correspondence; the only directional signal is term order plus shared Grade ancestry and trivial token overlap ('to', 'wri'/'tte'), which alone cannot establish developmental dependency. A symmetric relatesTo therefore fits better than a permitted Term 1 -> Term 2 buildsTowards. Both endpoints' source evidence lists are truncated (24 omitted items each) and ancestors carry merge/audit context, so deeper evidence of dependency may exist but is not present here.

However, the evidence shows two parallel, concurrently scheduled activity bullets with no extension, added complexity, greater independence, or staging of one toward the other, so a same-Grade/same-Term developmental claim is not substantively supported and buildsTowards is not warranted. The nomination signals (shared token 'to', trigrams 'own'/'rea', shared Grade/Term/Skill Area ancestors, page gap 1) are surface-level and were not treated as semantic evidence.
